title: Safety Culture and Human Factors

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A highway has a posted speed limit, and that sign is the policy. The culture is how fast people on that road actually drive, and whether a passenger feels comfortable saying 'ease up.' Those two things can be very far apart. Safety culture is the unwritten 'how we really operate here,' and it is what governs behavior at 3 a.m. when no supervisor is watching.

### Question 2

Three drivers each rear-end the same car. One hit a patch of black ice. One was following a little close because everyone on that road does and it never felt dangerous. One was racing a friend. The dented bumper looks identical in all three cases, but treating those drivers the same would be indefensible. Just culture asks what choice the person made, not how unlucky the outcome happened to be.

### Question 3

A USB-C cable plugs in no matter which way you are holding it, in the dark, one-handed. Someone made it symmetrical on purpose because they knew users would fumble it. That is human factors: instead of printing 'insert correctly' on the cable, the designer removed the wrong way. In hospitals the same reasoning gets applied to pump screens, tubing connectors, alarm sounds, and how a supply room is laid out.

### Question 4

A coach who never criticizes a missed shot is doing something smart, because players who fear the sideline stop taking shots at all. But 'we never say anything to anyone' collapses the moment someone deliberately trips an opponent. Just culture is the coach who says: missed shots, tell me what you saw, no consequences; deliberate tripping, that we address. Safe to speak, still answerable for choices.

### Question 5

On a flight deck, rank does not overrule the fuel system. If the person who actually knows how that system behaves is not the captain, a well-run crew still listens to them, and the captain's job becomes making sure that voice reaches the decision. On a unit, the aide who has been at the bedside for eight hours may hold the single detail that changes the plan. Deference to expertise means the operative question is 'who actually knows?' rather than 'who outranks whom?'

### Question 6

If ten different people trip on the same step, you can keep telling each one to watch their feet, or you can go look at the step. The systems question is 'what is it about this step?' Human factors specialists ask that deliberately, because correcting the walker never fixes the stair, and the eleventh person is already on their way up.

### Question 7

A pilot who hears one unfamiliar rattle does not wait for the engine to quit before investigating. That rattle is free information about something bending before it breaks. Preoccupation with failure means being the kind of team that chases the rattle, and equally the kind of team where the newest member feels entirely comfortable saying 'I heard something odd.' One without the other does not work.

### Question 8

A diesel nozzle is too wide to fit the filler neck on a gasoline car. You can be exhausted, on the phone, and holding it with one hand, and it still will not go in. Nobody had to read anything or remember anything. Compare that to a sticker on the pump reading 'check your fuel type,' which works only if you look at it and only if you are not already thinking about something else.

### Question 9

This survey is essentially asking every employee, anonymously, 'if you saw something wrong, would you actually say it out loud, even to someone above you?' A low score means a lot of people quietly answered no. That is not a report that harm has occurred yet; it means the batteries have been taken out of the smoke detector, and that is worth fixing before there is smoke.

### Question 10

If every roommate cuts across the freshly mopped floor because the long way takes forever, singling out one of them changes nothing for a week at most. The durable answer has two parts: talk to the person, and then move the mop bucket or prop the other door so the safe route stops being the annoying route. That pairing, conversation plus system change, is exactly how just culture handles shortcuts.

### Question 11

One person cutting across the grass is one person. A worn dirt track across the lawn where hundreds of feet have gone is not hundreds of rule-breakers; it is a sidewalk built in the wrong place. Landscape designers call those desire paths, and the good ones pave them. A workaround that nearly everyone uses is a desire path telling you the official route does not fit the actual job.

### Question 12

If a car chimed every time you touched anything, you would stop hearing the chimes within a week, including the one that means a door is open at highway speed. That is alert fatigue, and clicking 'OK' is not the same as reading. Adding warnings feels like action because it is visible and cheap, but attention is a finite resource, and real fixes change the machine or the task so the warning is not needed.
